sections.heading: Owning my careless prayer
sections.text: Lord of grace, I have often rushed through prayer or kept it shallow, especially when no one else sees. Please wake up my conscience so I feel how foolish and ungrateful that is. When I begin the day careless toward you, that first turning away easily pulls me into more sin. If I treat meeting with you as a small thing, it is right that I should feel the loss of the nearness I neglected.
theological_themes: Neglect of private prayer is not merely poor discipline but ingratitude toward God; sin often grows from small early compromises; God may lovingly let a believer feel the loss of communion when fellowship is treated lightly.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus assumes his disciples will pray privately before the Father, not only publicly or formally. This grounds the prayer’s concern with hidden, personal communion with God.
David asks God to search and expose what is wrong within him. That fits the request for a quickened conscience that can recognize careless prayer as sin rather than excuse it.

sections.heading: Remembering what I owe you
sections.text: Keep me from stealing from you the worship that belongs to you, and from starving my own soul by withholding it. Don’t let me forget that I was made to love you, honor you, and obey you forever. You are infinitely worthy of that. So when I fail to glorify you, my sin is not small. I have offended the God who deserves all love, and apart from your mercy I deserve your just judgment.
theological_themes: God is worthy of total love, honor, obedience, and worship; failing to glorify God is morally serious because sin is against the infinite worth of God; human beings are accountable before God’s righteous judgment.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus names wholehearted love for God as the greatest commandment. This supports the prayer’s language of an abiding duty to love, honor, and obey God.
Paul describes sin as a failure to honor God and give thanks to him, even when his reality is known. That matches the prayer’s claim that withholding worship is a real offense, not a minor omission.
Paul teaches that sin deserves death while eternal life is God’s gift in Christ. This gives biblical weight to the prayer’s sober acknowledgment of deserved judgment.

sections.heading: Asking for forgiveness and restored love
sections.text: Forgive me for the ways I have dishonored you. Soften the hardness in me. Heal the ways I keep drifting back. Open again a living fellowship of love between us. I don’t want to hide from you or merely feel bad at a distance; I want to come back to you as the God who receives repentant sinners.
theological_themes: Repentance seeks not only relief from guilt but restored fellowship with God; God forgives, heals backsliding, and receives those who confess their sins.

scripture_references.connection: John promises forgiveness and cleansing to those who confess their sins. This directly supports the prayer’s plea for pardon and restored fellowship with God.
God promises to heal his people’s apostasy and love them freely when they return. That illuminates the prayer’s request that God heal backsliding and reopen communion in love.

sections.heading: Letting your mercy lead me deeper into repentance
sections.text: When your compassion warms the cold places inside me, and your Spirit fills me, I see my sin more honestly. I am shocked at what still lives in me, and I hate the corruption I find there. Yet your grace does not make me careless. It draws me to repentance and gives me a stronger desire for real holiness from the inside out.
theological_themes: God’s mercy does not minimize sin; it exposes sin more deeply and motivates repentance; the Holy Spirit gives inward renewal and holiness rather than mere outward reform.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says God’s kindness is meant to lead sinners to repentance. This supports the prayer’s claim that grace and mercy are powerful motives for turning from sin.
Paul distinguishes godly grief that produces repentance from worldly sorrow. The prayer seeks that kind of Spirit-shaped grief: honest hatred of sin that moves toward God, not despair.
God promises to give his people a new heart and put his Spirit within them so they walk in his ways. This grounds the prayer’s longing for inward holiness through the Spirit’s work.

sections.heading: Bringing my heart under Christ’s blood
sections.text: Never let me forget that my heart is in your hands. When I sin, apply to me again the cleansing power of Christ’s atoning blood. Let your mercy pull me toward you, not away into shame or excuses. Make the cross the place where my guilt is answered and my heart is brought back to you.
theological_themes: God rules over and can change the human heart; Christ’s atoning death is the believer’s continuing hope when sin is confessed; mercy draws sinners near through the gospel.

scripture_references.connection: John writes to believers who still sin and points them to Jesus Christ as advocate and atoning sacrifice. This supports asking God to deal with fresh sin through Christ’s finished work.
Hebrews teaches that Christ’s blood cleanses the conscience so believers may serve the living God. That fits the prayer’s request for guilt to be answered and the heart restored to God.
This proverb teaches that God can direct even a king’s heart according to his purposes. It supports the prayer’s confidence that the petitioner’s own heart is also in God’s hands.

sections.heading: Freeing me from sin and lifting my soul to you
sections.text: Draw me away from everything evil. Put to death in me the love of the world that keeps competing for my heart. Teach me to live ready for the day I leave this life, humbled by repentance but encouraged by your love. My soul is often like a cart with no wheels, stuck in the heavy mud of sin. Lift me by your strength. Give me wings to rise toward you.
theological_themes: Sanctification includes being weaned from evil and putting worldly desires to death; penitence prepares the believer to face death with humility and hope; God alone can lift a sluggish, sin-clogged soul into renewed communion with him.

scripture_references.connection: Paul commands believers to put to death what is earthly in them. This supports the prayer’s request for God to mortify sinful desires and detach the heart from evil.
John warns against loving the world and its passing desires. This grounds the prayer’s longing to be weaned from worldliness and made loyal to God.
Paul speaks of death in light of being with Christ, not as denial or despair. That supports the prayer’s desire to be ready for departure from this life.

Isaiah describes the Lord renewing the strength of those who wait for him so they rise up like eagles. This directly illuminates the prayer’s final image of God lifting a stuck soul upward to himself.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s language that failure to glorify God is an “infinite evil” meriting “infinite punishment” reflects a classical Reformed account of sin measured by the infinite worth of God. I preserved the substance while expressing it in less technical language as sin against the infinitely worthy God deserving just judgment.

The original says it is just for God to “withdraw thy presence” from one who approaches him carelessly. To avoid implying that God abandons his adopted children, I rendered this as the believer rightly feeling the loss of neglected nearness or communion.

The phrase “deeply abhor myself” can be misunderstood today as self-hatred detached from grace. I rendered it as hating the corruption of sin found within, while keeping the original’s severe self-knowledge and repentance.

The request to be “mortified to the world” is culturally and theologically dense Puritan language. I interpreted it in the biblical sense of putting sinful desires to death and being freed from worldly loves, not as contempt for creation or ordinary human life.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated the prayer’s complaint about hasty private prayer as the opening sin from which the rest of the prayer flows, rather than as a general productivity or discipline issue.
I kept the progression from neglected prayer, to the seriousness of sin, to forgiveness, to Spirit-wrought repentance, to Christ’s atoning blood, to sanctification and readiness for death.
I interpreted “open an intercourse of love” as restored living fellowship and communion with God, since the original refers to relational nearness rather than a specific practice.
I preserved the concrete final images by keeping the stuck cart in mud and the eagle’s wings, because those images carry the prayer’s sense of spiritual helplessness and God-given renewal.
